21768-a-desert-drama:
Tourists on the Nile steamer Korosko sail from Shellal on February 13, 1895, in this adventure novel by A. Conan Doyle. The flat-bottomed boat is bound for Wady Halfa, past the first cataract of the Nile. Doyle frames the tale as a true incident long kept out of the papers for private and political reasons. He builds it from sworn statements, letters, and a secret inquiry at Cairo.

The pleasure trip turns to desert drama when danger closes on the party far from help. Doyle, already famous for Sherlock Holmes, brings the same tight craft to a tale of capture and rescue. Colonel Cochrane, Miss Adams of Boston, and Captain Archer of the Camel Corps anchor his cast of witnesses.
a-new-england-girlhood-outlined-from-mem:
Lucy Larcom outlines her own girlhood in Beverly, Massachusetts, from memory, writing for the young at the suggestion of friends, as her preface says. She dedicates the sketch to her girlfriends in general. The contents begin Up and Down the Lane, then Schoolroom and Meeting-House, the Hymn-Book, and Naughty Children and Fairy Tales.

Later chapters cover beginning to work, mill-girls' magazines, and reading and studying, and close with a move from the Merrimack to the Mississippi. Larcom had worked in the Lowell mills as a girl, and she writes of books, hymns, and sea air with equal love. Her memoir remains a gentle, exact picture of a New England childhood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabama:
Alabama, twenty-second into the Federal Union of America, lies north of the Gulf of Mexico, counting among the Gulf, or South Central, states. Tennessee lies north, Georgia east, the Gulf and Florida south, and Mississippi west. From north to south it measures 336 miles, east to west 148 to 200 miles. Its area is 52,250 square miles, 710 water and 51,540 land.

The state divides roughly into the Tennessee Valley, the mineral region, the cotton belt, and the timber and coast regions. Northern vegetation belongs to the temperate zone, southern to the semi-tropical. Fine hardwood and ordinary timber spread well over the whole state. The principal crop is cotton, yielding 1,249,685 bales in 1905 and giving the state third place in cotton production. The entry then traces Alabama's history and Catholic missions and institutions there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alma:
Alma is a Hebrew word for a young woman, married or not, and so differs from bethulah, a virgin. The interest in the word comes from the famous passage of Isaiah 7:14, 'the Alma shall conceive.' Various opinions are offered about the Alma in this verse is said to be Achaz's wife, the prophetess of Isaiah 8:3, or any young married woman. Such a woman, because of the promised victory of Judah, she could soon call her child Immanuel, God with us. Metaphorically, the Alma could mean the Chosen People.

The last view offered is the Virgin Mother of the Messiah, the reading St. Matthew 1:23 adopts and Christian tradition follows. The distinction matters because bethulah unambiguously means virgin, while alma leaves the question open, and Christian tradition reads the verse through Matthew's Gospel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ama:
Ama, or Amma, is a Semitic term for mother, adopted by Copts and Greeks as an honour title for religious women and ladies of high rank. Coptic inscriptions give it to both categories, and Greeks used it much as Latin used abbatissa, or abbess. Ama, or amula, also names a vessel receiving the people's wine offering for the Holy Sacrifice.

Pope Adrian I, who reigned 772 to 795, presented an ama to St. Adrian's Church. One word thus covers a title of reverence and a liturgical vessel, both rooted in early Christian usage.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-bayma: This 1913 reference article on Bayma — the Jesuit mathematician. Joseph Rickaby honors his scientific labors. His science probed the numbered laws. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loryma: This 1913 reference article on Loryma — an extinct Carian diocese. Sophrone Pétridès outlines its shadowy record. Ancient pastors tended the coastal faithful. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massa-maritti: This 1913 reference piece on Massa Marittima — the Tuscan diocese. Umberto Benigni gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Maremma flock. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mobile-alabam: Mobile, the old French port on the Gulf, became the Catholic metropolis of Alabama with its archdiocese. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-halm: Nicholas Halma was the French astronomer who translated Ptolemy's Almagest, giving modern scholars the ancient master in French. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicopolis-arm: Nicopolis of Armenia Prima was a city of the Anatolian highlands important enough to host a Christian bishop in the early centuries. This brief entry notes its site and its church history. A quiet name from the ancient map, its bishops recorded in the old lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nyssa-cappado: Nyssa was the see of St. Gregory, the great theologian brother of St. Basil. This entry covers its history, its famous bishop, and its church. The city of the younger Cappadocian: Gregory's theology shaped the Church's doctrine of the Trinity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oklahoma: Oklahoma's Catholic story runs from the Indian missions to the archdiocese of Oklahoma City. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and institutions. The faith in the Sooner State: its cathedral crowns Oklahoma City to this very day, proudly and visibly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osma: Osma, the Castilian see of El Burgo, was St. Dominic's first diocese before he founded his order. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The diocese that formed St. Dominic: its canons taught the young founder his theology and discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-panama: Panama became the archdiocese of the isthmus, bridging two oceans and two continents. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith at the crossroads of the world: its great canal would one day make it a global city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parma: Parma is the Emilian city of Correggio's domes and the great Farnese. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its art. The faith in the land of Parmesan: its cathedral guards Correggio's painted dome with true and lasting civic pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quadragesima: Quadragesima is the forty days of Lent's solemn fast. This entry explains its origin, its observance, and its liturgy. The Church's great retreat: its black ashes mark the penitent brow in Lent's first holy days of fast and prayer and tears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quinquagesima: Quinquagesima is the Sunday before Lent's Ash Wednesday. This entry explains its name, its liturgy, and its observance. The last feast before the fast: its last alleluia falls silent till Easter's bright dawn in April's holy joy and song and praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sasima: Sasima, the Cappadocian town of St. Gregory's exile, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Asia Minor: its bare ruins crown the hills in Cappadocia's plain in Turkey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-septuagesima: Septuagesima is the prelude of the Lenten fast. This entry explains its name, its liturgy, and its history. The ninth Sunday before Easter: its old name counts the seventy in the liturgy of Rome in the missal of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sexagesima: Sexagesima is the second prelude of Lent. This entry explains its name, its liturgy, and its history. The eighth Sunday before Easter: its old name counts the sixty in the liturgy of Rome in the missal of the Church in the West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sidyma: Sidyma, the Lycian city of the hills, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Asia Minor: its ancient ruins crown the hills in Lycia's highlands in the Taurus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sodoma: Sodoma was the painter of Siena's frescoes. This entry examines his canvases, his Monte Oliveto, and his fame. The master of the Sienese color: his great frescoes graced the abbey in the 1500s' decades in the cloister of the Olivetan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-rose-of-li: St. Rose of Lima was the Dominican tertiary. This long entry examines her penances, her Peru, and her fame. The first saint of the Americas: her tiny cell crowned Lima in the 1610s' Peru in the city of the kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tadama: Tadama was the titular see of Mauretania. This brief entry traces its ruins and its bishops. A vanished diocese of North Africa: its ancient ruins crowned Mauretania in the books of the geographers in the library of the old scholars.

govdocs-archive_org-PaulRassinierCollect:
Paul Rassinier, a French former concentration camp prisoner turned writer, published Debunking the Genocide Myth in French in the postwar years. This English edition came from Noontide Press in 1978. Adam Robbins translated it, and Pierre Hofstetter wrote the introduction. Rassinier questioned the scale and method of the Nazi murder of the Jews.

His study disputes the gas chambers and the accepted death toll, arguing from his own camp experience and selected documents. Historians have refuted his claims in detail, and the book is classed as a founding text of Holocaust denial. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for the study of that literature and its methods.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergManuscr: Harold Weisberg drafted manuscript pages on the investigation of James Earl Ray, the man convicted of killing Martin Luther King Jr. The draft follows a tracing job credited to a man named Jerry. Weisberg treated the Ray case with the same doubt he brought to the Kennedy case. The pages show him shaping evidence and argument before print, in draft form.
gulbadan-humayun-nama:
Princess Gulbadan Begum, daughter of Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, wrote the Humayun-Nama around 1587. Her nephew Akbar asked her to set down what she recalled of his father, Humayun. Anette Beveridge's 1902 translation is the version here.

Gulbadan tells of Humayun's reign, his exile, and his return to power in India. Because she lived inside the court, she records weddings, births, feuds, and household life that state histories skip. Hers is the only surviving Mughal-era history written by a woman. Its warm, direct voice makes the imperial family feel close and human. She writes of the women's quarters with detail no court historian could match.
joe-strong-the-boy-fire-eater-or-the-mos:
Joe Strong the Boy Fire-Eater is a circus novel for boys by Vance Barnum, published in 1916. Barnum also wrote Joe Strong, the Boy Wizard and Joe Strong and His Box of Mystery. Chapter one, The Vanishing Lady, opens under the big tent of the Sampson Brothers' Circus. Ringmaster Jim Tracy warms up the crowd for Professor Joe Strong.

Tracy boasts that Joe does more than hide eggs or pull rabbits from hats. A lady will sit in full view, then vanish into thin air, and no one will tell how. Joe stands center stage in a spotless suit of white silk tights. The title promises fire-eating as his most dangerous act. Barnum writes the circus as pure wonder for young readers.
lahoma:
John Breckenridge Ellis wrote the novel Lahoma, set in the American West. Its twenty-six chapters open with the touch of a child. A man called Brick makes the next move, then comes flight.

Chapter titles promise a mysterious guest, Red Feather, and getting civilized. A flag of truce and writing home suggest divided loyalties. Later chapters bring fences, a mob, and journey's end. Lahoma herself grows from child to young woman across the tale. Ellis mixes frontier danger with a warm story of raising a girl. Brick's rough frontier ways soften under the child's influence. Growth, not gunplay alone, carries the book to its close.
letters-to-his-son-complete-on-the-fine-:
The complete Letters to His Son gather Chesterfield's whole course of counsel. An editor's note explains old style and new style dating. England's Julian calendar lagged eleven days behind Europe's Gregorian one.

Chesterfield dated letters across that gap with careful marks. From Leipzig study to Paris salons, the letters follow one education. Manners, books, money, and company receive endless, polished advice. Critics have called the teaching cynical; admirers call it honest. Reading the whole run lets each reader judge that famous dispute. Later editors grouped the letters by year for readers. The complete run spans roughly a quarter century of advice.
memoirs-of-the-author-of-a-vindication-o:
William Godwin wrote Memoirs of the Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. J. Johnson and the Robinsons printed it in London in 1798. Chapter one covers the years 1759 to 1775 of her life.

Godwin holds that the dead of great merit are owed a true account. Calumny and false tales stick to such folk, he argues. A just life story can spur others to walk the same path. No subject, he says, touches the public weal more than hers. The public good, he argues, is bound up with such justice. Honor paid late still teaches the living how to aim.
nasa-tm-19630006259-performance-summary-:
John L. Allen, Owen H. Davis, and Glenn A. Mitchell of Lewis wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-149, in April 1960. It sums up tests of a supersonic air inlet. The inlet was a round, double-cone design built for Mach 3.0 flight. Two cones squeezed the incoming air from the outside.

The team ran the inlet from Mach 3.0 down to Mach 0.8. They tracked pressure recovery, air flow, cowl pressure, and extra drag. A jet engine starves if its inlet wastes pressure at speed. Off-design flight, slower than the design point, strains inlets most. This summary gave engine designers a full map of one bold inlet across its range.
nasa-tm-19680013998-proposed-standards-d:
J. E. Decastra and F. E. Wells, of the Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this February 1968 memorandum, TM X-53692. The pair set out to give missile plumbing leaks a shared, standard language. Under their plan, any worker who finds a leak can describe its size in numbers that others will read the same way.

The work covers the theory behind leak checks and the test gear and steps used to find leaks. Drawings sort threaded and flange leaks into classes, with charts for the ranges between them. An appendix gives the full procedure for describing and estimating leaks in aerospace plumbing. The aim was one clear standard for inspection, testing, and evaluation crews.
nasa-tm-19690018461-a-functional-random-:
Iwao Hosokawa wrote this Goddard preprint, numbered X-641-68-180 and dated May 1969, on a functional random-walk model of the many-particle system. Statistical mechanics follows huge crowds of particles that sit away from equilibrium, still settling toward balance. Hosokawa recasts that hard problem as a kind of random walk, the mathematics of wandering steps.

Transforming his state functional formalism for the BBGKY hierarchy gives the new view, he writes. The basic equation then sits very close to the classic Fokker-Planck form. A slight change turns it into a universal master equation with irreversibility built in. The wandering quantity becomes particle density across the single-particle state space. A general solution is formulated for the weak interaction case.
nasa-tm-19710011693-thermodynamics-of-th:
Lawrence Flax of the Lewis Research Center wrote this theory paper for a spring 1971 physics meeting in Cleveland. It extends the Heisenberg model of a ferromagnet to cover an applied magnetic field. A ferromagnet keeps a lasting magnetic pull, like iron. Near its Curie point, that pull fades as heat turns the material paramagnetic.

Flax worked in the random phase approximation for the uniform case. He studied heat related values near the Curie point. They include magnetization, susceptibility, and how fast magnetization changes with temperature. An outside field lifts magnetization above its zero field value. It also shifts the critical point, and the paper follows both effects.
nasa-tm-19720021198-a-discussion-of-co-a:
Mikio Shimizu of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this discussion in June 1972, numbered X-620-72-209. It treats carbon monoxide and loose oxygen atoms on Venus and Mars. Both planets wear carbon dioxide skies. Sunlight splits that gas into carbon monoxide and oxygen. The puzzle is why the two products do not simply rejoin at once. Shimizu examined chemistry that keeps the balance steady. The paper runs to twenty four pages.

On Venus, carbon dioxide soaks up key ultraviolet light. That shade slows the breakdown of another gas, hydrogen chloride. Chlorine freed there speeds the rejoining of oxygen and carbon monoxide. Related chlorine compounds may tint the Venus haze yellow. Mars shares much of this chemistry in thinner form. The discussion weighed these linked reactions for both planets.
passages-from-a-relinquished-work-from-m:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's "Passages from a Relinquished Work" appeared in his collection Mosses from an Old Manse. The narrator looks back on his boyhood in the home of a village parson who raised him alongside his own three sons. The guardian is remembered under the nickname Parson Thumpcushion, earned by pounding his pulpit cushion while he preached.

The narrator admits the parson's strict rule made his three sons respectable men, while he himself went astray. He tells his own wandering course with dry humour and some regret. The piece reads like a fragment of a life story Hawthorne chose not to finish.
piccolissima:
Piccolissima was translated from the French of Adélaïde de Montgolfier by Mrs. Follen, who signs her preface at Brookline in October 1857. Montgolfier, she notes, was the daughter of the celebrated inventor of balloons. Her fanciful story is, in fact, a little lesson in natural history, and she vouches for the truth of all Piccolissima reports of the insects she meets.

The heroine descends, on her father's side, from the famous Tom Thumb, and on her mother's from a princess who once lodged in a spectacle case. Through her tiny adventures, children learn the manners and customs of insects.
podcast-dannyjones-a2DuoICk4mA:
Young crypto founders who call themselves the Blockchain Boy visit Danny Jones. They run a media firm named Cryptonite. Their partner Michael Sessa joins as chief leader of the venture.

The title claims a teenage fortune made in the metaverse. The guests describe media work tied to coins and virtual worlds. Jones asks how young men built wealth so fast. They explain deals, hype, and timing in a wild market. The episode captures peak crypto confidence, useful now as a record of how that boom sounded from inside. Skeptics will hear plenty to question as well.
podcast-joerogan-BYVQfLi6wMA:
Former television host Steve Hilton joins Joe Rogan for episode 2542. Hilton advised a British prime minister before moving to America. He later worked in California politics and media.

He brings an insider's view of a state at a crossroads. Rogan asks how policy shaped the California dream and its fade. Hilton argues that rules and costs pushed people out. The talk ranges over populism and party failure. Listeners get a British-born analyst reading America's largest state with both love and alarm. His accent only sharpens the outsider's edge he brings.
sakoontala-or-the-lost-ring-an-indian-dr:
Kalidasa wrote Sakoontala, or The Lost Ring, an Indian drama. Sir Monier Monier-Williams translated it into English prose and verse from the Sanskrit. The title page names him as Boden Professor of Sanskrit. It also names him as a fellow of University College and late fellow of Balliol College, Oxford. In his preface to the eighth edition he notes that the translation, first issued in 1855, has gone through seven editions. That record, he admits, might fairly have freed him from the duty of revising it.

Three years before, he heard that Sir John Lubbock had given Sakoontala a place among the hundred best books of the world, and had adopted his version. Monier-Williams therefore went through every line again and compared the translation with the Sanskrit.
sienkiewicz-without-dogma:
Sienkiewicz turned from vast epics to one man's inner life in Without Dogma, here in English. His hero, a rich and clever aristocrat, keeps a diary of his doubts. He can analyze all things yet cannot quite believe or love with his whole heart.

The diary form lets readers watch a mind trap itself with its own cleverness. Faith, love, and duty all slip through his fingers as he watches. Sienkiewicz called men like him a sign of the age's sickness of soul. The book is his most searching and somber novel, a portrait of modern unbelief from within.
tecumseh-a-drama: Charles Mair wrote Tecumseh as a drama. A quote from Tecumseh's speech to the Osages opens the book. It tells how the first white men came hungry and weak to Native shores. The cast names Tecumseh, chief of the Shawanoes. His brother the Prophet stands beside him. His wife Mamatee and his niece Iena also appear. The American side names General Harrison and General Hull. Harrison was governor of Indiana Territory.
the-darrow-enigma:
Melvin L. Severy's The Darrow Enigma is built as a set of episodes. They are The Episode of the Darkened Room, of the Sealed Document, of Rama Ragobah, of the Parallel Readers, and of the Taletale Thumb. Each episode is split into chapters. A motto asks what we shall say when dream-pictures leave their frames of night and push us from the waking world.

The narrator casts himself as a passive observer rather than an actor in the events. He is a physician, a graduate of a Western university. His practice is now large thanks to a singular blunder into fame: a cure he worked in the now celebrated case he is about to tell. A year earlier, he confesses, he had little enough to do.
the-doctor-s-dilemma: Hesba Stretton's novel The Doctor's Dilemma, printed in New York in 1872 by D. Appleton and Company, is present here only as a title page and contents list. Two parts of plain numbered chapters are named, with no chapter titles at all. The narrative itself is absent here. The two-part frame alone suggests a life split by one hard choice in a doctor's world of sickness and faith.
the-drama:
Henry Irving's The Drama gathers four addresses by the famed actor-manager. The contents name The Stage as It Is, The Art of Acting, and Four Great Actors, with a frontispiece by Whistler. In the first address, given at Edinburgh on November 8, 1881, Irving defends the living stage against those who claim to prize Shakespeare more in print than in play.

Such claims, he says, are cheap pride and fear of the theatre's name. Irving speaks as a working actor for his craft's worth. The talks still show how the stage argued its case.
the-growth-of-english-drama: Arnold Wynne wrote The Growth of English Drama. Wynne held the degree M.A. The Clarendon Press at Oxford printed the book. This impression is dated 1927; the first edition was 1914. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in six chapters. The chapters run from Early Church Drama and English Miracle Plays through Moralities and Interludes. One treats comedy in Lyly, Greene, Peele, and Nash. One treats tragedy in Lodge, Kyd, and Marlowe. An appendix treats the Elizabethan stage.
the-lone-wolf-a-melodrama: Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Lone Wolf, dated 1914. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The nineteen chapter titles sketch a melodrama's arc: Troyon's, Return, A Point of Interrogation, A Stratagem, Anticlimax, and The Pack Gives Tongue. L'Abbaye, The High Hand, Disaster, Flight, Confessional, Sheer Impudence, and Restitution follow, closing with Unmasked. French place names and the pack imagery suggest a lone operator hunted by a group, though the chapters themselves cannot be read in what is present.
the-moving-picture-boys-at-panama:
Victor Appleton's The Moving Picture Boys at Panama is dated 1915. Its subtitle reads Stirring Adventures Along the Great Canal. Only a frontispiece caption, title page, and contents are present here, so the adventure does not appear. The frontispiece shows earth crashing out from under Joe's feet as he stood on it.

Twenty-five chapters are listed. To the Rescue and On the Brink open the tale, followed by surprises, a delayed letter, and a trip through New York toward Panama. The Little Box and The Secret Conference lead into scenes along the canal, in the jungle, and in Culebra Cut. An emergency dam, a big slide, Gatun Dam, and Mr. Alcando's disappearance fill the closing headings.
the-moving-picture-girls-or-first-appear:
First Appearances in Photo Dramas opens Laura Lee Hope's series The Moving Picture Girls. Only title page and a partial contents list are present here. The sisters' story itself does not appear. Grosset and Dunlap held the 1914 copyright, and the World Syndicate Publishing Company issued the book at Cleveland and New York. A frontispiece caption shows Alice and Ruth holding the stage alone in one scene.

Five chapters are listed with page numbers. An Unceremonious Departure opens at page 1, Russ Dalwood Apologizes at page 11, and The Old Trouble at page 20. Despondency and Replaced close the visible list. Hope's Bobbsey Twins and Outdoor Girls books are advertised on the title page.
the-road-to-mandalay-a-tale-of-burma: B. M. Croker's tale of Burma was first published by Cassell in October 1917 and reprinted three times before a popular edition of 1919, dedicated to a late Royal Munster Fusiliers colonel. Contents move from blinds down and a closed house through kicks and halfpence, clouds, an empty offer, and a monster toward a ship bound for Burma and the land of promise. Here only the title pages, dedication, and opening of the chapter list are present, so the Burmese story itself does not appear.
the-true-woman-a-series-of-discourses-to:
The Rev. J. D. Fulton of Tremont Temple, Boston, published The True Woman in 1869, a series of discourses with Woman versus Ballot added. His preface says the book grew from that lecture's reception: well received by the majority, it met strong opposition from those rejecting the place assigned to woman in the Word of God. Fulton turned more and more to the scriptural argument. He concluded that the campaign to win women the ballot sprang from infidelity to the Word, and to woman herself.

His discourses trace Eve as God made her, the helpmeet; woman as tempter, despoiled of glory; and woman restored through Christ to equality in the church. Fulton writes against women's suffrage from the pulpit at the movement's early height. Historians of that fight will find the opposition's biblical case stated in its own confident terms.
thelma: Marie Corelli's novel Thelma is represented here by a contents list alone, covering Book I and the start of Book II. Chapters run in Roman numerals, paired across two columns without titles. No chapter text follows the list in what is present. Readers can see the book's scale and two-book shape, but none of Corelli's story itself. Only the front listing is present here, so the chapters do not appear.
two-men-of-sandy-bar-a-drama: Bret Harte's Two Men of Sandy Bar survives here through its cast list, headed The Prodigals. Sandy, son of Alexander Morton senior, shares the bill with John Oakhurst, his former partner, who is personating Sandy himself. The cast adds a detective called Capper, an Australian convict named Pritchard, and the Duchess, illegally married to Sandy. Only the dramatis personae are present here, so the drama itself does not appear.
wagner-s-tristan-und-isolde-an-essay-on-:
George Ainslie Hight wrote his essay on Wagner's Tristan und Isolde for readers new to the composer, under lines of Walt Whitman about a victorious song in the night. His preface owns that the pages hold little that is new, and nothing to interest those already at home in Wagner's work. They speak to beginners who want to know what Wagner aimed at and how his operas differ from those that came before.

No English book he knows of, Hight says, gives a beginner that start. An introduction is needed, not because Wagner's works are artificial, but because our minds have been bent by the highly artificial wares of Italian and French opera houses. Against that training, a Wagner drama at first seems strange. Readers get a patient guide to the music drama, its aims, its methods, and its demands on the ear.
